body.text: Fidel Castro’s birth centenary (1926-2026) this year offers a fresh opportunity to examine his pivotal role in the emergence of post-Revolution Cuban cinema. Not since Lenin did any head of state do more than Castro to explore the possibilities of cinema not only to chronicle the achievements of a new, radically different political order, but also the areas of endeavour where more positive work remained to be done. While the thrust was mainly on the documentary, the fictional feature laced with the documentary also figured in the agenda.

If the eclectic documentarist Dziga Vertov was entrusted with the responsibility of making the world aware of the relevance of the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917, a similar job was cut out in post-1959 Cuba for Santiago Álvarez, who had, ironically, gone to the US to make money but returned to his homeland, his head buzzing with socialism, having witnessed from close quarters how capitalism actually works.

If Tomás Alea was the most distinguished figure in the ranks of the older generation of Cuban filmmakers, arguably the most prominent among those who came on the heels of the old guard was Humberto Solás, who died of cancer on September 17, 2008. But while Alea chose to work on a variety of themes and subjects (witness Memories of Underdevelopment, Death of a Bureaucrat, Up to a Point, The Last Supper, Strawberry and Chocolate, et al), Solas is identified more than anything else with what he himself called “historical melodramas” enacted in the context of Cuban political, social, artistic, and personal realities in the 20th century.

Owing to the peculiar circumstances in which the Cuban revolutionary society came to see the light of day, the country’s filmmakers had to take upon themselves the role of the fledgling nation’s conscience keepers. Humberto Solás was a member of the first generation of directors to mature following the Revolution of 1959. Born into a humble Havana family, Solas chose to be an urban guerrilla while still in his teens and abandoned formal studies altogether. As he was to explain later: “It was a very unstable time to try to study. Either Batista (Cuban dictator) closed down the university, or we did.”

Prior to the Revolution, chances of being a filmmaker seemed like an unrealistic dream to Solas. However, he managed to make a short film and was invited to join the Cuban Film Institute (Instituto Cubano del Arte e Industria Cinematográficos, ICAIC) soon after its founding in 1959, as a typist. The expectation of the authorities was that whilst typing out other people’s handwritten scripts, the new entrant would benefit in many ways, mainly politically and aesthetically. The ICAIC was destined to play a monumental role in the growth of authentic people’s cinemas throughout the Latin American continent.

At the same time, the ICAIC also gave opportunities to filmmakers and students of cinema from Africa and Asia to teach, learn, discuss, and grow. From time to time, the ICAIC, pioneered by the likes of the great Argentine neo-realist Fernando Birri, the Colombian writer and cineaste Gabriel Garcia Márquez, and Cuba’s home-grown Julio García Espinosa, iconic for his ardent advocacy of an “imperfect cinema”, invited Indian filmmakers to participate in its programmes, including Mrinal Sen and Anand Patwardhan. In time, India’s most important and best-known documentarian was to hail the arrival of Espinosa’s “hand-held, black-and-white grainy, fast-moving footage bearing the marks of the struggle it depicted”.

Although it was customary for Cuban directors to serve an extensive apprenticeship in documentaries characterised by a certain social perspective and a detailed scrutiny of popular experience, Solás made some early fiction shorts as well. But he was conscious that these films carried reflections of cultural inferiority and alienation in the materially underdeveloped world. These are feelings often engendered even in the most gifted artists of the three colonised and neo-colonised continents, awed by the supposed strength and superiority of European and Western film styles. About this phase of his career, Solás had ruefully observed: “Neither me, nor my generation, nor my country can be seen in any of these films.”

It was this critical realisation that caused Solás to approach Cuban realities with a new consciousness. His choice of historical subjects followed as an inevitable corollary. According to him, the importance attached to historical films in Cuba (like Sergio Giral’s The Other Francisco, Octavio Gómez’s The Charge of the First Machete, or his own Lucia, which tells the stories of three women belonging to three different periods in the chequered and tumultuous history of Cuba—the 1890s, the 1930s, and finally the 1960s—is due to our history being filtered in earlier times “through a bourgeois lens”. Solás: “We lack a coherent, lucid, and dignified appreciation of our national past.” In calling his own films “historical melodrama", the director was trying to attain a Marxist perspective capable of providing a materialist interpretation to historical events and to individual psychology.

Significantly, Solás, like his great peer Pastor Vega, famous for his Portrait of Teresa featuring his renowned actress-wife Daisy Granados, frequently identified women as a central metaphor in his films because he believed that as a dominated group, women feel more deeply and reflect more immediately the contradictions in society. For instance, the contradiction of continued existence of Latin machismo in revolutionary Cuban society, Solás’ classic critique of machismo in the final part of Lucia will continue to be used for a long time to come as a reference point in any serious discussion on this huge negative issue in the collective psychology and individual behaviour in Latin societies. In this connection, Solás said: “The sad masquerade of limited, archetyped, and suffocating human relations in defence of private property is most transparent in the case of women—half of humanity. The pathetic carnival of economic exploitation begins here.”

Needless to emphasise, it does not speak highly of the West’s ability to appreciate film art that Solás did not make the grade, so to say, in that part of the world till he directed Un hombre de éxito (A Successful Man), which came to be selected for the best foreign-language Oscar. Be that as it may, A Successful Man rightly gained many admirers worldwide. Here, Solás attended to a characteristically broad canvas covering political history, personal goals, and emotional relationships, all the while pursuing an aesthetic of impassioned experimentation. The film’s story covers a crowded period of about 30 years and effectively contrasts the private lives and public careers of two brothers separated by ideology and ambition.

A Successful Man portrays many of the artistic and ideological concerns with which Solás was commonly identified. A scathing critique of the political and psychological evolution of men and women in turbulent times, their methods as much as their morals, A Successful Man carries haunting echoes of universal experience even as it relates a quintessential Cuban story. The saints, thieves, fools, cowards, heroes, madonnas, whores, and “successful men and women” populating this small masterpiece have their imitations walking the streets, lurking in the shadows, warming unlikely beds, climbing the ladder, or taking their own lives in any place on the face of the earth; and, sometimes, as Solás reveals with a chilling clarity, they eke out successful lives of a deathly pallor. By the time the film ends, the viewer may well be asking himself along with the director—Who is the successful man—the one who lives by and dies for his ideals, or the one who survives by betrayal, only to die a little each day?

The revolutionary experience/experiment in Cuban cinema being what it is, it is perhaps inevitable that filmmakers in the small Caribbean island should still be visible in the role of political thinkers and ideologues; as critical propagandists and creative pamphleteers. During his 1987 visit to New Delhi as head of the jury at the International Film Festival of India (IFFI), Solás was asked for his reaction to the problems that the cinemas of the three continents (many inadvisedly call them the Third World) have to routinely face vis-à-vis the entrenched and dominant interests of Hollywood and European cinemas. Solás’ reply is clearly as relevant today as it was four decades ago.

He said: “Although the so-called Third World is heterogeneous, I can talk about the Latin American Cinemas. The greatest problem that we face is distribution. It is incredible that we produce so many films and yet we face problems of distribution, precisely because all the distribution channels are manipulated by North American distributors. For example, a Bolivian can have as many problems in seeing an Argentine film as he will have in seeing an Indian film. But now we have the Foundation of New Cinema in Latin America based in Havana which, among other things, has the objective of acquiring as many Latin American films as it can and also of buying at least one theatre in every Latin American country. It is a fairly dramatic situation because, for example, in Venezuela, one sees a Latin American film only if it has won an Oscar or an award at Cannes. Cuba is the only country where films from all Latin American countries can be seen because we ourselves are in control of the distribution system.”
US hostility and sanctions

The gains of the revolutionary experiment, impressive as they are, are of course far from complete. Admissions to that effect from time to time by the Cuban political and intellectual leadership are significant. At the same time, widespread awareness about the areas of weakness impeding the process of nation-building points to a mature and struggling people committed to shaping their destiny along extremely difficult alternative lines. It goes without saying that art and culture in general, and cinema in particular as envisaged and translated into reality after 1959 have played a compelling role in the fashioning of that destiny. If contemporary Cuban cinema continues to show signs of both resistance and resilience, it is at least partly due to a growing realisation in the nation’s political circles that new strategies have to be devised to take on the current winds of threats and renewed sanctions emanating from Washington.

Any other country, big or small, would have wilted under American pressure in a matter of years, if not months, but the Cubans, strong not just in their own resolve but bolstered by some amount of external support, have refused to yield. Words and sometimes deeds of assurance from individuals or groups of artists in different parts of the world have no doubt acted as a balm and a boon to the beleaguered nation that has been struggling against American pressures ever since February 1962 when John F. Kennedy, using his presidential powers high-handedly and in total violation of accepted democratic norms, imposed the first trade and economic sanctions to bring the “upstarts” to their knees. But no American President has been so consistently fiendish, so brutal, nasty, and short, in his efforts to undo the life and legacy of the Cuban Revolution as Donald Trump.

Not a day passes without the roughneck bombast, in his second term of presidency, threatening Havana with the very worst. Perhaps, what makes it worse for the socialist regime is the string of victories notched up by extreme right-wing nominees of Trump in different Latin American countries from Argentina and Chile to Bolivia and Peru to Colombia and Ecuador. Whereas, in earlier times, the Left or Centre-Left-leaning governments in these countries had been unmistakably comradely in their relations with Cuba, the present political leaderships have turned hostile on their own initiative or on the instructions of Washington. All the time, the tragic example of an “annexed” Venezuela looms before their eyes.

Cinematic replies, perhaps “rebuttals” would be a more appropriate word to use, to US economic sanctions have been many. At least one of them may be discussed here considering that it came from a distant land underlining the international reach of the legacy of the Cuban Revolution. In 2011, the reputed Serbian documentarist Goran Radovanović came up with a beautiful and intensely believable journey into the soul and spirit of the threatened nation. Making common cause with the tested idea that nothing is more precious than independence and honour to a people like the Cubans, placed as they are in the midst of a revolutionary process, Radovanović calls his 50-minute colour film, With Fidel Whatever Happens (2011).

In keeping with his earlier films like the delightfully sad Chicken Elections (2005) about an old grandmother devoted to her chickens who is unable to vote in an impending election because she dies on the eve of the event, Radovanović’s Cuban film is characterised by a striking fusion of strong socio-political content with an impressive devotion to experimenting with narrative forms. The way he drives himself to reach the limits of a unique personal film language is nothing if not amazing. The director can be dead serious in his engagement with realism, but he can also be deliciously ironic to drive home his views on life in general, on art, on specific social issues, and on an array of individual responses to popular upheavals.
The Sierra Maestra spirit

Episodic in structure, for the most part realistic in style, and relying more on long- and mid-shots than close-ups to create a distancing effect so as to guard against a cloying sentimentality, the film is situated in Sierra Maestra, a settlement 850 kilometres east of Havana. The director chooses the day before the celebration of the 52nd anniversary of the Revolution to tell his story of resistance and attempted recovery. The characters chosen from the crowd, so to say, to tell the ongoing story of the Revolution, are deeply involved in what they are doing, sometimes at some amount of personal discomfort.

An old man is shown repairing a motorcycle that had seen its best days many summers ago; again, a young dentist makes his way to a clinic in a remote mountain first on foot, followed by riding a donkey, and later still, a bus that rattles more than it moves, to keep an appointment with anxious patients, one of whom is improbably named Vladimir Ilyich Rodriguez (reminds one of the occasional Lenin or Stalin still walking the roads of Keralam and Tamil Nadu); and, finally, there is a middle-aged couple who share their telephone on a daily basis with their neighbours who don’t have one, perhaps in remembrance of a dearly loved lost child whose framed photograph adorns the drawing room. These stories of sharing can perhaps be read as an attempt to understand how and why the popular uprising of 1959 has survived, however shakily, to this day, complete with minor hiccups and major setbacks, along with recoveries and renewals as well.

Radovanović: “The fate of these people (like the old man, the dentist, and the couple) and many other inhabitants of Sierra Maestra, is depicted on a day of ideological ecstasy … And the following day? The next day, driven by inertia, they all return to the rhythm of everyday life which is the same and is not very promising. Everyone is aware of that. Even the bullhorns that constantly blast out ideological slogans that are 52 years old … But the Revolution continues.”

The images in Radovanović’s film tell tales of destitution and decay, but they also speak of defiance; of a resolute will to pick up the bits and pieces and carry on the journey. Nothing seems to work—public transport is in a ramshackle condition, food is scarce and expensive, people go about with frayed looks and in frayed dresses—but the nation refuses to grind to a halt. Its schools, hospitals, and recreation centres keep moving slowly, falteringly, to a desired destination that may take a few more generations to reach, provided bullying Uncle Sam doesn’t in the meantime come visiting militarily. With humour, a little sadness, a touch of anger, and much hope and patience, Cubans are walking the path to fulfilment. The director, thanks to his cinematic skills and political maturity, keeps us glued to his film as he unveils the sentiments of a people in transition.
Bread, roses, and the war

Come to think of it, Cuba is fighting one of the longest wars in the history of Man. Since January 1, 1959, that is, for the past 67 years, every day has been a day of bitter conflict between a clever and brave beetle manoeuvring itself in countless ingenious and statesmanlike ways so as not to get crushed underfoot by a rogue elephantine aggressor. True, bullets have not been flying in this war, bombs have not been dropped from the air, but even more sinister weapons have been let loose aiming at the jugular of the little island. Here, it may sound bizarre, but it is true that more than one filmmaker has used the medium to bring out the “beneficial effects” of this seemingly endless war. If a long line of delinquent American Presidents, both Democrats and Republicans, from Kennedy to Trump, had not been so desperate to destabilise the anti-capital, pro-poor, radical regime in Havana, perhaps the Cuban people and their leaders would have never known of the lengths to which they could go to preserve the gains of the Revolution, currently under the worst siege it has known since its inception.

Radovanović spent some of the most difficult years of his life experiencing the prolonged fratricidal war that ended with the splintering of Yugoslavia. He should be especially qualified to depict attitudes of individual and collective opposition to unwarranted and unacceptable belligerence, be it in the nature of a civil war or a confrontation imposed on a country from without. The aesthetics of patience that Radovanović employs in With Fidel Whatever Happens not only heightens the effectiveness of the statement he wishes to make, but also adds to the pleasure and satisfaction of watching the film. The imaginative use of local earthy music is a key component in the creation of the film’s aesthetic beauty.

An early female socialist had said that the poor and the deprived need both bread and roses, perhaps in that order. She did not spell it out, but it can be imagined that the “roses” she spoke of denoted as much romantic love as the love many common people have for their society and the land of their birth. In With Fidel Whatever Happens, Radovanović gives us touching glimpses of some ordinary Cuban lives informed by as much tenderness as tension, the latter a fallout of a relentless quest for an alternative model of human growth, existence and empowerment where individual self-worth and love of national sovereignty are more important than the acquisition of creature comforts by any means. Somewhere along the line, the taste of freedom blends deliciously with that of sausages being bought from a wayside vendor by men, women and children returning home after attending the Independence Day celebrations.
Vidyarthy Chatterjee writes about cinema, society, and politics. His most recent book is called About Nothing in Particular (Aksharik, Kolkata).
